2.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **tenth generation**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [to generation number ten] or [after ten successive generations, he]

3.note: Moses says **until forever** as an extreme statement for emphasis. In this context, it does not mean literally “for eternity” but rather refers to an indeterminate future time, specifically for ten generations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [for all generations to come] or [permanently]

4.note: The phrase **on account of the matter that** introduces the reasons for God’s command that the Ammonites and Moabites could not enter the assembly of Yahweh. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a connecting word or phrase that shows that the information that follows gives the reasons for the prohibition that came before. Alternate translation: [because]
The word **you** is plural here, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **bread and water** represent food and drink in general. Moses uses these basic items to refer to all the provisions that travelers would need. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with provisions] or [with the food and drink you needed]
The words **Balaam** and **Beor** are the names of men. Balaam was a prophet, and Beor was his father.
The name **Aram Naharaim** means “Aram of the two rivers” (Euphrates and Tigris) and is in the region later called “Mesopotamia.”

Here, **to curse you** marks this phrase as the goal or purpose of the Ammonites and Moabites hiring Balaam. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to curse you] or [with the intention of cursing you]

5.q: וְ⁠לֹֽא־אָבָ֞ה יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֣עַ אֶל־בִּלְעָ֔ם וַ⁠יַּהֲפֹךְ֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֧י⁠ךָ לְּ⁠ךָ֛ אֶת־הַ⁠קְּלָלָ֖ה לִ⁠בְרָכָ֑ה כִּ֥י אֲהֵֽבְ⁠ךָ֖ יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽי⁠ךָ
5.note: The word **because** introduces the reason for what came before. If it would be clearer in your language, you could reverse the order and put the reason first. Alternate translation: [Yahweh your God loved you, so he was not willing to listen to Balaam and turned the curse into a blessing for you]

5.q: יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ & יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֧י⁠ךָ & יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽי⁠ךָ
5.note: See how you translated the phrase “Yahweh your God” in 1:10.

Moses uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the Ammonites’ and Moabites’ intention to curse Israel and Yahweh’s refusal to allow it. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, Yahweh your God was not willing to listen to Balaam]

By **was not willing to listen to Balaam**, Moses means “would not do what Balaam said.” See the discussion of “listen” in the Introduction to Deuteronomy for further information about this. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh your God would not do what Balaam asked] or [But Yahweh your God refused to do what Balaam wanted]

5.q: וַ⁠יַּהֲפֹךְ֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֧י⁠ךָ לְּ⁠ךָ֛ אֶת־הַ⁠קְּלָלָ֖ה לִ⁠בְרָכָ֑ה
5.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **curse** and **blessing**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh your God changed what would have harmed you into what helped you]

6.note: Moses is referring to any good things by naming two major components, **peace** and **prosperity**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their well-being] or [anything good for them]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **peace** and **prosperity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [for them to live peacefully or to prosper]

Moses is using **all your days, to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “continuously throughout all time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all time to come] or [perpetually]

7.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [You shall not detest an Edomite because he is your brother]

Here Moses is speaking of an Edomite as if he were actually a **brother** to an Israelite. He means that the Edomites were descendants of Esau, who was the brother of Jacob, the ancestor of the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for he comes from our relative Esau]

The word **because** introduces the reason for the command not to detest Egyptians. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since you were foreigners in the land of Egypt, do not detest the Egyptians]

8.note: Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [descendants that are born to them] or [children that are born to them]

The expression **are born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The sons who become part of their families] or [The sons who come from their families]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **the third generation**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [after three generations]

10.note: Here, **a man** represents any man in general, not a specific man. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any man] or [anyone]

Moses is referring to a man having a nocturnal emission in a polite way by using the phrase **not clean, happening at night**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [who becomes unclean because of something that happens while he sleeps] or [who has a bodily discharge during the night]

11.note: The word **himself** indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same person fills two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [he shall bathe in water]

13.note: The term **spade** refers to a digging tool. In this context, it may have been a small shovel or simply a stick that soldiers would carry with them to dig holes and cover their excrement. If your readers would not be familiar with this kind of tool, you could use the name of a similar tool that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and you shall use a digging tool]

Moses is referring to defecating in a polite way by using the phrase **sitting yourself out**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [when you relieve yourself] or [when you go to attend to your needs]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and put the dirt back]

14.note: **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. This verse gives the reason for all the instructions about cleanliness in verses 1–13. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before.

Here Moses is speaking of **Yahweh** walking **in the midst of your camp** as if God were physically moving around in the Israelite camp. This image represents God’s active presence with his people and his close involvement in their affairs. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh your God is present among you in your camp] or [Yahweh your God is actively watching over you in your camp]

Here, **to give you victory and to give your enemies to your faces** marks the goal or purpose of **Yahweh your God walks in the midst of your camp**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to make you victorious and to deliver your enemies into your power]

The phrase **to your faces** represents “into your power” or “into your presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and to give your enemies into your power] or [and to deliver your enemies to you]

Moses is using the phrase **and turn away from you** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the Israelites an instruction to keep their camp holy so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [or else he will turn away from you] or [lest he turn away from you]

15.note: Here Moses is not referring to a specific **slave**. He means slaves in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any slave]

16.note: Here the term **gates** refers to the entire city or town. See how you translated the similar phrase “within your gates” in 5:14. Alternate translation: [in one of your towns]

Moses is using **as good to him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “as he pleases” or “wherever he wants.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [wherever he pleases] or [wherever he wants to live]

17.note: The term **cultic prostitute** refers to someone who engaged in sexual acts as part of the worship of pagan gods. This practice was common in ancient Canaanite religion but was forbidden in Israel. If your readers would not be familiar with what a cultic prostitute is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [woman who performs sexual acts in pagan worship … man who performs sexual acts in pagan worship] or [female temple prostitute who serves false gods … male temple prostitute who serves false gods]

18.note: Moses assumes that readers will know that he is referring to a male prostitute by using the word **dog**. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [or money earned from a man who sells himself for sex]

Moses is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into Yahweh’s temple] or [into the sacred temple of Yahweh your God]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [when making any vow] or [to fulfill any vow to Yahweh]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [are detestable to Yahweh your God] or [greatly offend Yahweh your God]

19.note: See how you translated “to your brother” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [but to your fellow Israelite] or [but to another Israelite]

19.q: נֶ֥שֶׁךְ כֶּ֖סֶף נֶ֣שֶׁךְ אֹ֑כֶל נֶ֕שֶׁךְ כָּל־דָּבָ֖ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִשָּֽׁךְ
19.note: Moses uses a repetitive series of clauses in **interest of money, interest of food, interest of each thing that is charged interest** to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming. Alternate translation: [interest of any kind at all]

Here Moses is using the term **brother** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

20.note: Moses is not referring to a specific **foreigner**. He means non-Israelites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to any foreigner]

Here, **so that** marks **Yahweh your God may bless you** as the goal or purpose of the instruction about charging or not charging interest. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that Yahweh your God may bless you]

Moses is using **in all the sending out of your hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in everything that you do” or “in all your activities.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in all your activities]

21.note: Moses is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [you make a solemn vow]

21.q: כִּֽי־דָּרֹ֨שׁ יִדְרְשֶׁ֜⁠נּוּ יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ מֵֽ⁠עִמָּ֔⁠ךְ וְ⁠הָיָ֥ה בְ⁠ךָ֖ חֵֽטְא
21.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because Yahweh your God will surely require it from you, and it would be sin for you]

Moses is repeating forms of the verb **require** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Yahweh your God will absolutely require it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and you would be sinning]
The pronoun **it** refers to not fulfilling the vow. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and not fulfilling the vow would be sin for you]

22.q: וְ⁠כִ֥י תֶחְדַּ֖ל לִ⁠נְדֹּ֑ר לֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֥ה בְ⁠ךָ֖ חֵֽטְא
22.note: The implication is that if someone does not make a vow to God, they cannot be guilty of breaking it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [But, if you do not make a vow, you will not sin because you will not have a vow to fulfill]
See how you translated “sin” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [you would not be sinning]

23.q: מוֹצָ֥א שְׂפָתֶ֖י⁠ךָ & נְדָבָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּ֖רְתָּ בְּ⁠פִֽי⁠ךָ
23.note: The phrases **What has gone out from your lips** and **a vow that you have spoken with your mouth** mean similar things. Moses is using these expressions together to emphasize the binding nature of spoken vows. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this with a single phrase at the beginning and leave the second phrase off. Alternate translation: [What you have solemnly promised]

Moses is using **What has gone out from your lips** as a common expression of his culture to mean “what you have promised.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What you have promised] or [The promise you have made]

The terms **keep** and **do** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [you shall absolutely fulfill]

24.note: Moses is using **as your spirit is satisfied** as a common expression of his culture to mean “as much as you want.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as much as you want to eat] or [until you are satisfied]

A **vessel** is a kind of container. If your readers would not be familiar with what a vessel is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [your basket] or [your bag]

25.note: Here, **stalks** represents the grain growing in a field. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the grain field of]

A **sickle** is a kind of curved blade with a handle that people use to cut grain. If your readers would not be familiar with what a sickle is, you could use the name of a similar tool that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [but you shall not use a harvesting blade] or [but you shall not use a cutting tool]
